title: Juz' 'Amma, again
hook: the thirtieth part, now heard with five years behind it
tomorrow: how do you keep reading one book for the rest of your life?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Insan: givers who wanted no thanks, and, one commentator said, never even said so. For his sake. Today, back to the short surahs.
screen: `FOR HIS SAKE.` → `BACK TO THE SHORT SURAHS.`

segments.voice: A song learned at eight sounds different at eighteen: the same words, and suddenly a line about leaving lands hard. The last part of the Qur'an can work like that. It holds the short surahs at the back of the book, the ones a child can carry by heart: al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq, an-Nas, al-Asr. It takes its name from the first word of its first surah, 'amma: about what? About what are they asking one another? Five years on this path, and the short surahs come back. With them comes an old argument: is it better to hold many by heart, or a few by meaning?
screen: `A SONG AT EIGHT, AT EIGHTEEN.` → `'AMMA: ABOUT WHAT?` → `MANY BY HEART, OR A FEW BY MEANING?`

segments.voice: One view says: carry as much as you can. The words themselves are the gift. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the one skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who stumbles through it, finding it hard, gets a double reward. Every surah held by heart is one you can pray with anywhere: on a bus, in a hospital, with no book and no phone. Memory is a home the words can't be evicted from. The other view says: slow down and understand. The Qur'an asks, in Surah Muhammad, whether people will not ponder it, or whether there are locks on their hearts. Another verse calls it a scripture sent down so that people would reflect on its verses. On this view, three surahs you understand will change you more than many you only pronounce. Both views have teachers behind them. The steelman for memory: understanding grows later, and you can't reflect on words you don't have. The steelman for meaning: a surah recited without a single thought behind it is a beautiful sound passing through. Some teachers join the two: hold the words now, and open them for the rest of your life. And the short surahs make that case themselves. Al-Asr is a few lines about time and loss. Al-Ikhlas, a few lines about who God is. A child can hold them. A grown-up can spend years inside them. The first part you knew is still the part you're learning.
screen: `VIEW ONE: CARRY THE WORDS.` · `A DOUBLE REWARD FOR STUMBLING.` · `VIEW TWO: LOCKS ON THE HEARTS?` · `HOLD THEM NOW, OPEN THEM LATER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST PART YOU KNEW.`

segments.voice: If you know three short surahs by heart, say them aloud now, slowly, the way you first learned them. If you know fewer, say what you know, and leave a pause after each line to ask what it means. If you know none, sit with one question al-Asr raises: what does time take from us, and what doesn't it take?
screen: `THREE SHORT SURAHS, ALOUD.` · `A PAUSE AFTER EACH LINE.`

segments.voice: Juz' 'Amma: the last part of the Qur'an, named for its first word, 'amma, about what. The short surahs, heard again.
Your line: the first part you knew. It's still teaching you, five years on. Juz' 'Amma, heard again.

howItsDone: Muslim children are often taught the short surahs of Juz' 'Amma early, and they're recited in the daily prayers; Muslim teachers encourage both memorizing the Qur'an and reflecting on its meaning.

fork.setup: your cousin, nine, asks: 'why should i memorize surahs if i don't understand them yet?' give the memory side's best case.
options: you'll carry the words anywhere, and the meaning can grow into them later.

fork.reveal: that's the steelman: Sahih Muslim gives a double reward to the one who struggles, and memory gives meaning a place to grow. the other side would add: then open them, for life.
